candidates.attacker_control: The path portion of an HTTP request URI (raw, percent-encoded form) once the request is routed to a ResourceHttpRequestHandler; or, for the legacy servlet, the `resource` request parameter (?resource=...). Attacker fully controls the encoding and the placement of '%XX' sequences and path separators.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The snapshot already contains substantial hardening: ResourceHttpRequestHandler.isInvalidPath rejects WEB-INF/META-INF, ':/'-style URL paths, and '..' that survives StringUtils.cleanPath; getResource performs a percent-decode re-check; PathResourceResolver enforces class equality and an allowed-locations check and re-decodes resource paths containing '%'. I verified that ordinary single- and double-encoded '../' payloads are rejected by these checks, and that the filesystem/servlet-context APIs used by createRelative (ClassPathResource/ServletContextResource/UrlResource/FileSystemResource) generally do not themselves decode '%XX', which limits many payloads. No tests or runtime execution were performed; the concrete bypass therefore remains unverified and configuration-dependent.
candidates.impact: Unauthenticated read/streaming of files that were not intended to be exposed: files outside the configured static-resource directories (config, secrets, source), arbitrary web-application resources via the ResourceServlet `resource` parameter (including anything reachable by a RequestDispatcher include), i.e. information disclosure; the same path handling is also the mechanism of the known CVE-2016-9878 directory-traversal issue fixed in the 4.3.5 timeframe.
candidates.prerequisites: Web MVC application configured to serve static resources through ResourceHttpRequestHandler (addResourceHandler/addResourceLocations, <mvc:resources/>, or a ResourceHttpRequestHandler bean), or an application exposing the deprecated ResourceServlet. Exploitation also depends on container/proxy behavior that preserves encoded or control-character sequences in getRequestURI() (the code path uses UrlPathHelper's single decode of the raw URI, not the container-normalized path) and, for the strongest variants, resource locations declared without a trailing separator or a Windows filesystem where trailing/embedded characters are normalized.
candidates.root_cause: Request-derived paths are validated as raw strings rather than as normalized/resolved paths. ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource() runs processPath()/isInvalidPath() on the path and then only a single URLDecoder.decode() re-check; the decoded value is not re-run through processPath()/isInvalidPath(), so control characters left inside path segments hide '..' from StringUtils.cleanPath() (e.g. a decoded segment such as '\u0000/../' is not recognized as '..' because the token is not exactly '..'), and the value actually used for resolution is always the un-normalized string. PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation() then accepts a resource using an un-normalized string prefix comparison (resource.getURL().getPath()/getPath() startsWith cleanPath(location) + '/'), and its percent-decoding check is skipped when the raw path contains no '%' and only looks for the literal '../' once. The same class of flaw exists in the deprecated ResourceServlet.doInclude(), which passes the user-supplied `resource` parameter straight to HttpServletRequest.getRequestDispatcher(url).include(...) with no path validation when allowedResources is not configured.
candidates.title: Static-resource path validation gap allows traversal outside configured resource locations (ResourceHttpRequestHandler / PathResourceResolver / ResourceServlet)
candidates.trace: DispatcherServlet -> SimpleUrlHandlerMapping.lookupHandler (AbstractUrlHandlerMapping.java:161-221) exposes PATH_WITHIN_HANDLER_MAPPING_ATTRIBUTE = AntPathMatcher.extractPathWithinPattern(pattern, lookupPath) after UrlPathHelper.decodeAndCleanUriString (UrlPathHelper.java:421-426) -> ResourceHttpRequestHandler.handleRequest -> getResource: processPath + isInvalidPath (lines 406-412), one URLDecoder.decode re-check (413-426) -> DefaultResourceResolverChain -> PathResourceResolver.getResource (120-134) -> location.createRelative(resourcePath) -> checkResource/isResourceUnderLocation (146-203) with raw-string startsWith and single decoded '../' test -> resource returned to handleRequest and streamed to the client by ResourceHttpMessageConverter. For ResourceServlet: doGet (196-230) -> determineResourceUrl (240-242) -> doInclude (270-290) -> request.getRequestDispatcher(url).include(...).
candidates.unverified: No end-to-end exploit was demonstrated. The exact combination (encoding depth, container behavior, location separator, filesystem platform) required to reach a file outside the configured location was not proven from source alone, and the fix-window attribution to the 4.3.5 static-resource hardening is inferred from the snapshot version (4.3.5.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, dependency dates) rather than from patch metadata. ResourceServlet behavior with allowedResources set is constrained; without it, exposing the servlet is required.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

coverage_summary: Scope: 3,885 model-visible Java/build files in the assigned spring-framework snapshot (main sources only; no src/test trees), filters per get_source_scope (no binary or sensitive-path exclusions reported; parity with B0). Relation index: index_status complete, 3,885/3,885 files indexed, 43,485 symbols, 82,540 calls, 88,657 edges, 720 facts; qualification states candidates are syntactic/navigation hints with no data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof, and unsupported analyses are simply absent, so unreported areas were not treated as reviewed. I read in full or in relevant part: spring-webmvc resource-serving stack (ResourceHttpRequestHandler, PathResourceResolver, ResourceServlet, ResourceHandlerRegistry, AbstractUrlHandlerMapping, AntPathMatcher, UrlPathHelper, StringUtils.cleanPath/applyRelativePath, core Resource implementations), spring-messaging simp broker/subscription classes, and spot-checked CORS/multipart/remoting/deserialization call sites via text search. Areas only sampled, not audited line-by-line: spring-expression internals, spring-jdbc/orm/tx, spring-websocket transport, portlet module, XML/config parsers, and the large remaining spring-context/spring-beans surface.
limitations: No build, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source reading.
Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so fix-revealing test cases could not be consulted.
No git history or patch metadata is available, so the mapping of the snapshot to a specific fix commit/CVE is inferred (version 4.3.5.BUILD-SNAPSHOT plus Dec-2016 dependency dates) and uncertain.
The P1 index provides navigation hints only; it does not prove data flow or reachability, and unsupported analyses are omitted rather than reported.
Exploitability of the submitted candidate depends on servlet-container URI handling, resource-location configuration, and filesystem platform, none of which can be evaluated from source alone.
Large modules (spring-oxm, spring-jdbc/orm, spring-websocket transports, spring-context internals) were not exhaustively audited for additional issues.

rejected_leads.lead: spring-messaging DefaultSubscriptionRegistry evaluates the client-supplied STOMP `selector` native header as a SpEL expression against a StandardEvaluationContext (addSubscriptionInternal parses it at lines 139-161; filterSubscriptions evaluates it at lines 188-231 with new StandardEvaluationContext(message)). This is a direct untrusted-input-to-expression-evaluation flow that can permit method invocation / T(...) type access and thus remote code execution in apps using the simple broker, and it matches the later CVE-2018-1270.
rejected_leads.reason: Strong source evidence and high impact, but not submitted because only one candidate is allowed and the snapshot version (4.3.5.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, Dec 2016) does not align with that fix window; exploitability also requires a STOMP-over-WebSocket endpoint with the in-memory broker and a subscribed client.

rejected_leads.lead: spring-context/spring-core remote invocation exporters deserialize Java objects from the network (RemoteInvocationSerializingExporter.doReadRemoteInvocation -> ObjectInputStream.readObject, line 139-142; CodebaseAwareObjectInputStream; ConfigurableObjectInputStream in spring-core).
rejected_leads.reason: Dangerous-by-design deserialization in HttpInvoker/remoting, but it is a documented architectural property of these APIs rather than a bounded input-validation defect, and no fix exists in this snapshot's window; not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: spring-webmvc-portlet PortletUtils/DispatcherPortlet uses request.getResourceID() to obtain a PortletRequestDispatcher (PortletUtils.java:516-521).
rejected_leads.reason: Guarded by PortletUtils.isProtectedResource(id) and portlet-container semantics; no strong evidence of a bypass in source.

summary: Spring Framework 4.3.5.BUILD-SNAPSHOT (Dec 2016, maintenance branch 4.3.x): I reviewed the static-resource serving stack and other high-risk modules. The strongest source-evidenced candidate is incomplete validation of request-derived resource paths in spring-webmvc (ResourceHttpRequestHandler.getResource/isInvalidPath/processPath and PathResourceResolver.isResourceUnderLocation, plus the unvalidated `resource` parameter of the deprecated ResourceServlet), which is the code family fixed in the 4.3.5 timeframe (CVE-2016-9878). The existing hardening (WEB-INF/META-INF and ":/" checks, cleanPath-based ".." check, one URLDecoder re-check, allowed-locations check) is real, so this is a lead, not a confirmed exploit. A second, technically very strong but unselected lead exists in spring-messaging (SpEL evaluation of the STOMP `selector` header); it is noted below rather than submitted because only one candidate is allowed and its fix window does not match this snapshot's version.
